title: Bast AI evidence library
source: Copied verbatim from the Bast research canvas 'Bast AI evidence library: explainability, caregiving, who pays' (checked and updated October 28, 2026), including its study type and sample size fields. Internal usage notes and internal planning sections are intentionally not in this public repo. Five entries added November 3, 2026 with Beth Rudden's approval: A23, A24, A25, A26 and C9. Two entries added November 4, 2026 with Beth Rudden's approval: A27 and A28. Four entries added November 6, 2026 with Beth Rudden's approval: A29, A30, A31 and B14. Six entries added November 10, 2026 with Beth Rudden's approval: A32, A33, A34, A35, A36 and B15. Eleven entries added November 15, 2026 with Beth Rudden's approval: A37, A38, A39, A40, A41, A42, B16, B17, B18, B19 and B20. B12 removed November 15, 2026 with Beth Rudden's approval because the paper was retracted.

A.label: AI that shows its work keeps people thinking instead of offloading

B.label: Easing caregiver and care-worker burden improves patient outcomes

strengthDefinitions.Strong: An RCT, a randomized experiment or a meta-analysis of trials.
strengthDefinitions.Moderate: A cohort, reader study, quasi-experiment or review of observational studies.
strengthDefinitions.Limited: A survey, qualitative study, narrative review or self-report.
strengthDefinitions.Policy fact: Shows who pays, not whether something works.
strengthDefinitions.Vendor / unreviewed: Published by a vendor; not peer-reviewed.
strengthDefinitions.Preprint: Posted before peer review; not yet peer-reviewed.

directionDefinitions.Complicates: Cuts against it or limits it.

studies.title: LLMs alone vs people using LLMs
studies.finding: Tested alone, LLMs named the relevant condition in 94.9% of cases. Members of the public using the same LLMs got there in fewer than 34.5%, and picked the right next step in fewer than 44.2%. That was no better than a control group using their usual sources (the control group was better at naming conditions).
studies.source: Bean et al., Nature Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Randomized, preregistered study; 1,298 UK adults; 10 medical scenarios; GPT-4o, Llama 3, Command R+
studies.caveats: Written scenarios, not real patients. Lay public, not clinicians. It tests the human-AI handoff, not explainability directly. 'Field' here means a person using the tool, not a hospital rollout.
studies.whyItMatters: A capable model is not enough – care tools must help people reason through the answer, which is why AI should show its work.

studies.title: Neonatal X-ray AI: experts vs trainees
studies.finding: With a reliable-looking AI, radiology residents accepted 52.0% (13/25) of its wrong calls, vs 20.0% for pediatric radiologists and 33.3% for neonatologists. With a deliberately flawed AI, neonatologists overrode 91.7% (66/72) of its errors.
studies.source: Lee et al., npj Digital Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Multi-reader crossover reader study; 14 readers; 125 radiographs from 11 hospitals; 1,750 reads
studies.caveats: Only 3 neonatologists took part, and the authors call the 91.7% result hypothesis-generating. Retrospective, web-based, one diagnosis. The 91.7% (neonatologists overriding a deliberately flawed AI) and the 52.0% (radiology residents accepting wrong calls from a reliable-looking AI) come from different study arms and measure different things, so they are not a head-to-head comparison. Per-group figures come from the authors' public code repository.
studies.whyItMatters: Trainees trust confident AI the most, so tools for care teams must expose their reasoning and make errors easy to catch.

studies.title: Colonoscopy deskilling
studies.finding: After endoscopists started using AI, their adenoma detection rate in colonoscopies done without AI fell from 28.4% to 22.4% (a 6.0-point drop).
studies.source: Budzyń et al., Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology
studies.designAndSize: Multicentre observational before/after; 1,443 non-AI colonoscopies in Poland
studies.caveats: Observational before/after, so it cannot prove AI caused the drop; other things changed over time. An erratum was published.
studies.whyItMatters: Clinicians who lean on AI can lose their own skill, so AI should keep people thinking instead of doing the thinking for them.

studies.title: Mammography automation bias
studies.finding: When the AI suggested the wrong BI-RADS category, correct ratings fell from 79.7% to 19.8% for inexperienced readers, 81.3% to 24.8% for moderately experienced, and 82.3% to 45.5% for very experienced radiologists.
studies.source: Dratsch et al., Radiology
studies.designAndSize: Prospective reader experiment; 27 radiologists; 50 mammograms
studies.caveats: Small sample. The 'AI' was simulated (researchers set its suggestions). Lab reading, not live screening.
studies.whyItMatters: Wrong AI advice pulls even experienced readers off course; showing the evidence behind a suggestion gives clinicians a way to push back.

studies.title: BCG 'jagged frontier'
studies.finding: On 18 tasks inside AI's abilities, consultants with GPT-4 completed 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, with significantly better quality; bottom-half-skill consultants gained the most. On a task just outside AI's abilities, the control group was correct 84.5% of the time vs 60% and 70.6% in the two AI groups, an average drop of 19 percentage points.
studies.source: Dell'Acqua et al., Organization Science 37(2):403-423, DOI 10.1287/orsc.2025.21838 (earlier HBS working paper 24-013, 2023)
studies.designAndSize: Preregistered randomized field experiment; 758 BCG consultants
studies.caveats: Consulting tasks, GPT-4 in 2023, one firm. Quality was graded by people. Only one task outside the frontier.
studies.whyItMatters: AI lifts work inside its strengths and misleads people outside them, so users need to see where its reasoning holds.

studies.title: Epic Sepsis Model, external validation
studies.finding: The widely used proprietary sepsis model had an AUC of 0.63, missed 67% of sepsis cases (1,709 of 2,552), and still alerted on 18% of all hospitalized patients.
studies.source: Wong et al., JAMA Internal Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Retrospective cohort; 27,697 patients, 38,455 hospitalizations at Michigan Medicine
studies.caveats: One health system; sepsis definitions vary between studies.
studies.whyItMatters: A widely deployed model missed most sepsis cases; care teams need tools that show how they reach an alert.

studies.title: Sepsis model before clinicians act
studies.finding: The same sepsis model scored AUROC 0.62 overall but 0.47 (worse than a coin flip) once predictions made after clinicians had already recognized sepsis were removed.
studies.source: Kamran et al., NEJM AI
studies.designAndSize: Retrospective cohort; 77,582 hospitalizations
studies.caveats: One health system; retrospective.
studies.whyItMatters: Much of a sepsis model's apparent skill came after clinicians had acted, so teams should check what an alert adds before trusting it.

studies.title: Google diabetic retinopathy AI in Thailand
studies.finding: In the first six months in Thai clinics, 393 of 1,838 eye images (21%) were rejected as ungradable, driven by lighting, no dilation drops and equipment problems.
studies.source: Beede et al., CHI (Google Health)
studies.designAndSize: Field observation and interviews with nurses in 11 clinics
studies.caveats: Qualitative field study, not an accuracy trial. Lab accuracy figures are not reported in the same study.
studies.whyItMatters: Real clinics break lab-perfect AI; tools for care teams must fit the workflow and explain their failures.

studies.title: Pneumonia X-ray model across hospitals
studies.finding: A chest X-ray pneumonia model scored AUC 0.931 inside its own hospitals but 0.815 at an outside hospital. The models could tell which hospital an image came from (99.95% for NIH images).
studies.source: Zech et al., PLOS Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Cross-sectional study; 158,323 radiographs from 3 hospital systems
studies.caveats: Older models; retrospective.
studies.whyItMatters: Models can learn shortcuts, like which hospital took an image, so explanations help teams spot reasoning that will not travel.

studies.title: Dermatology AI on diverse skin
studies.finding: Three published skin-cancer models dropped from reported ROC-AUCs of 0.88 to 0.94 down to 0.56 to 0.67 on a new, biopsy-confirmed diverse image set, and did worst on dark skin.
studies.source: Daneshjou et al., Science Advances
studies.designAndSize: Retrospective evaluation on the DDI dataset (diverse skin tones)
studies.caveats: Image test set, not a clinical deployment. Fine-tuning on diverse images closed the skin-tone gap.
studies.whyItMatters: AI that fails on dark skin shows why care teams must see how a model reasons and where it was tested.

studies.title: How FDA-cleared AI is tested
studies.finding: 126 of 130 FDA-cleared AI devices (2015 to 2020) were evaluated only on retrospective data; none of the 54 high-risk devices had a prospective study; 93 reported no multi-site evaluation.
studies.source: Wu et al., Nature Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Review of FDA summaries for 130 devices
studies.caveats: Based on public FDA summaries; devices through 2020.
studies.whyItMatters: Most cleared AI devices were never tested prospectively, so care teams should demand evidence and transparency before relying on them.

studies.title: Explanations did not rescue a biased model
studies.finding: Clinician accuracy was 73.0% at baseline; a normal AI raised it 2.9 points (4.4 with explanations). A systematically biased AI cut it 11.3 points, and adding image explanations only partly helped (9.1-point drop; the 2.3-point difference was not significant).
studies.source: Jabbour et al., JAMA
studies.designAndSize: Randomized clinical vignette study; 457 hospitalists, NPs and PAs
studies.caveats: Vignettes, not live care. Tested heat-map style image explanations only.
studies.whyItMatters: Explanations did not protect clinicians from a biased model – showing work helps when the underlying model is sound.

studies.title: Explanations raised blind acceptance
studies.finding: Explanations made people more likely to accept the AI's answer whether it was right or wrong. Accuracy rose when the AI was right, fell when it was wrong, and team accuracy was no better than just showing the AI's confidence.
studies.source: Bansal et al., CHI
studies.designAndSize: Randomized online experiments; 1,626 crowd workers; 3 tasks
studies.caveats: Lay tasks (review sentiment, LSAT questions), not clinical.
studies.whyItMatters: Explanations can make people accept AI answers blindly; showing work must be designed to invite checking, not deference.

studies.title: Cognitive forcing (useful friction)
studies.finding: Asking people to decide first, request the AI, or wait cut over-reliance compared with simple explanations: when the AI was wrong, following it fell from 64% to 48% and correct answers rose from 8% to 27% (carb-source task). People liked these designs less.
studies.source: Buçinca, Malaya & Gajos, CSCW
studies.designAndSize: Randomized online experiment; 199 participants; nutrition task
studies.caveats: Lay task, simulated AI. Forcing reduced but did not remove over-reliance. Helped people high in 'need for cognition' most.
studies.whyItMatters: Built-in friction, like deciding before seeing the AI, keep people thinking and cut over-reliance.

studies.title: When explanations do help
studies.finding: Explanations reduced over-reliance when they made checking the AI cheaper than trusting it; hard-to-read explanations did not help.
studies.source: Vasconcelos et al., CSCW
studies.designAndSize: 5 randomized online studies; 731 participants; maze task
studies.caveats: Lab task with a simulated AI.
studies.whyItMatters: Explanations help when they make checking the AI easier than trusting it – the design target for AI that shows its work.

studies.title: Annotated AI advice helps non-specialists
studies.finding: AI advice with a visual annotation on the X-ray produced the highest diagnostic accuracy, and physicians who were not task experts benefited the most.
studies.source: Gaube et al., Scientific Reports
studies.designAndSize: Randomized online experiment; 223 physicians (117 IM/EM, 106 radiology)
studies.caveats: All advice was correct, so it does not test whether annotations help people catch AI errors.
studies.whyItMatters: Annotated advice helped non-specialists most, a direct case for AI that shows care teams what it sees.

studies.title: Skin cancer: who gains, who gets misled
studies.finding: Good AI support beat AI or physicians alone, and the least experienced clinicians gained the most. Faulty AI misled clinicians at every level, including experts.
studies.source: Tschandl et al., Nature Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Reader studies across expertise levels
studies.caveats: Reader studies on images, not live care.
studies.whyItMatters: Good AI support made clinicians better and faulty AI misled them all, so care teams need ways to see when the AI is wrong.

studies.title: Experience doesn't predict who benefits
studies.finding: Across 140 radiologists and 15 chest X-ray tasks, years of experience, subspecialty and AI familiarity did not reliably predict who benefited from AI. Wrong AI predictions hurt performance.
studies.source: Yu et al., Nature Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Large reader study; 140 radiologists
studies.caveats: Reader study, not live care.
studies.whyItMatters: Experience does not tell you who benefits from AI, so every user needs tools that make the AI's reasoning visible.

studies.title: AI tutors with and without guardrails
studies.finding: Students with plain GPT-4 scored 48% higher on practice problems but 17% lower on a later exam without AI than students who never had it. Students with the guardrailed tutor scored 127% higher in practice, and on the exam they were statistically indistinguishable from students who never had AI.
studies.source: Bastani et al., PNAS
studies.designAndSize: Randomized field experiment; nearly 1,000 high school math students
studies.caveats: Education, not healthcare; one country and subject. The guardrailed tutor avoided measurable harm but did not improve exam scores, and its students thought they had learned more than they had.
studies.whyItMatters: Unguarded AI raised practice scores and lowered real learning; guardrails that keep people thinking preserved skill.

studies.title: Customer support: novices vs experts
studies.finding: An AI assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average, 34% for novice and low-skilled agents, with minimal impact on experienced agents.
studies.source: Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond, NBER (published in QJE 2025)
studies.designAndSize: Staggered rollout, quasi-experimental; 5,179 support agents
studies.caveats: Productivity, not accuracy or learning. Numbers are from the NBER working paper; the 2025 journal version's figures may differ slightly.
studies.whyItMatters: AI helped novices most and experts little, so care tools should teach as they assist rather than replace judgment.

studies.title: Confidence in AI and critical thinking
studies.finding: Knowledge workers with more confidence in GenAI reported less critical thinking; those with more self-confidence reported more.
studies.source: Lee et al. (Microsoft Research), CHI
studies.designAndSize: Survey; 319 knowledge workers; 936 real work examples
studies.caveats: Self-report, cross-sectional. Correlation only.
studies.whyItMatters: More trust in AI meant less critical thinking, so care tools should keep users engaged with the reasoning.

studies.title: MASAI mammography trial (AI that worked)
studies.finding: AI-supported screening found 6.1 vs 5.1 cancers per 1,000 women, with the same 1.5% false-positive rate and 44.3% less radiologist reading.
studies.source: Lång et al., Lancet Oncology
studies.designAndSize: Randomized controlled trial; 80,033 women in Sweden
studies.caveats: Interim safety analysis; the interval-cancer endpoint came later.
studies.whyItMatters: Well-tested AI can lift cancer detection and cut workload – a reminder that strong evidence, not explainability alone, earns adoption.

studies.title: Correct advice helps novices most
studies.finding: Correct explainable AI advice improved diagnostic performance (OR 1.84) and confidence compared with no AI, most of all for novices. Clinicians also followed wrong advice, and ignoring correct advice cost more accuracy than following wrong advice.
studies.source: Gaube et al., The Lancet Digital Health
studies.designAndSize: Preregistered randomized crossover; 125 clinicians (50 radiologists, 75 novices) reading head CTs
studies.caveats: Scans were read in 2023, not in live care.
studies.whyItMatters: Explained advice helped novices most, and clinicians also followed wrong advice – showing work needs safeguards against both over- and under-reliance.

studies.title: Better notes, similar outcomes
studies.finding: Clinical notes improved with the LLM (appropriate diagnosis aOR 1.74). Treatment failure within 14 days was 2.2% with the LLM vs 2.0% without (aOR 0.77, not significant).
studies.source: Agweyu et al., Nature Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Cluster-randomized trial; 103 clinical officers; 16 Nairobi-area clinics; 9,691 patients
studies.caveats: A general LLM helper in one clinic network, not a tool built to show its work.
studies.whyItMatters: Better AI-assisted notes did not change treatment failure, so care teams should measure patient outcomes, not documentation polish.

studies.title: Explanations raised confidence, not trust
studies.finding: Narrative explanations raised confidence more than no transparency (P = .024) or numeric scores (P = .0051). Neither numeric confidence nor narrative explanations with citations moved trust (P = .68). The group with no transparency changed its diagnoses more (P = .0006).
studies.source: Frank et al., JAMIA
studies.designAndSize: Randomized experiment; 220 clinicians in three groups: no transparency, numeric confidence, or narrative explanations with citations
studies.caveats: Simulated vignettes, not live care.
studies.whyItMatters: Narrative explanations raised confidence without changing trust, so transparency features need testing against real decisions.

studies.title: Do AI agents trust their users?
studies.finding: Do LLMs and agents trust the humans they work with? The authors built 2,000 synthetic contrastive conversations and used activation steering across six open models. Turning trust up raised compliance with harmful requests. Turning trust down in tool outputs cut prompt-injection success from 33.6% to 7.1% on Qwen3.5-27B in AgentDojo, with capability within 2.7 points at moderate settings. How much an assistant relies on unverified claims, such as a caregiver saying medications were given, is a hidden setting that can be made explicit.
studies.source: Lasnier, Froger, Lasbordes and Seddah (Inria Paris / Sorbonne), arXiv
studies.designAndSize: 2,000 synthetic contrastive conversations; activation steering across six open models
studies.caveats: Tested on synthetic conversations and agent benchmarks.
studies.whyItMatters: How much an AI agent trusts its user shapes what it will do, a design question for any assistant in care settings.

studies.title: The open web is closing to AI
studies.finding: An audit of 14,000 web domains found that in one year (2023–2024), robots.txt restrictions fully blocked 5%+ of all tokens in the C4 training corpus and 28%+ of its most actively maintained, critical sources. Counting terms-of-service restrictions, 45% of C4 is now restricted. Health example: The Lancet's robots.txt (https://www.thelancet.com/robots.txt, checked Nov 4, 2026) disallows the whole site to 19 AI agents, including live user-fetch agents like ChatGPT-User and MistralAI-User, not only training crawlers.
studies.source: Longpre et al. (Data Provenance Initiative), "Consent in Crisis: The Rapid Decline of the AI Data Commons", NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (DOI 10.52202/079017-3431)
studies.designAndSize: longitudinal audit of robots.txt and ToS across 14,000 domains behind the C4, RefinedWeb and Dolma corpora
studies.caveats: Measures training-crawler blocking through April 2024.
studies.whyItMatters: Sources are closing to AI training, so care tools that cite open, traceable evidence become more valuable.

studies.title: Cloudflare blocks AI crawlers by default
studies.finding: On July 1, 2025, Cloudflare made blocking AI crawlers its default unless they pay creators, and said a majority of leading publishers had joined. Cloudflare estimates it is 750 times harder for a creator to get traffic from OpenAI than it was from Google in the past, and 30,000 times harder from Anthropic. McKnight's (https://www.mcknights.com/robots.txt), a senior-care trade outlet, uses Cloudflare's managed AI blocklist.
studies.source: Cloudflare blog (Matthew Prince), "Content Independence Day: no AI crawl without compensation!"
studies.designAndSize: company announcement with Cloudflare network traffic estimates
studies.caveats: Cloudflare sells the blocking product, and its figures come from its own network.
studies.whyItMatters: Content owners are blocking AI crawlers, raising the value of AI that cites and pays for the sources it uses.

studies.title: Fine-tuning improves how models report confidence
studies.finding: Supervised fine-tuning on GPT-4.1-mini and Llama-3.1-70B cut within-domain calibration error (ΔECE −0.57) and raised correct/incorrect discrimination (ΔAUC +0.17) across knowledge, math, and trivia tests, with some transfer to held-out medical, legal, and truthfulness sets. Multitask training generalized further.
studies.source: Steyvers, Belem & Smyth, Communications AI & Computing, Nov 5
studies.designAndSize: Model experiments on GPT-4.1-mini and Llama-3.1-70B
studies.caveats: Better calibration is the model grading its own confidence more accurately – not independent verification of the answer. Independent checking requires different thinking patterns and external evidence.
studies.whyItMatters: Models can learn to report confidence more honestly, a building block for AI that tells care teams when to double-check.

studies.title: Clinical translation and independent validation in medical AI
studies.finding: A systematic review of 247 medical-AI studies in selected 2024–2025 clinical and translational journals found retrospective design in 158/247 (64.0%), demographic or geographic limits in 50.6%, and no qualifying independent external validation in 28.7%.
studies.source: Wang et al., Cell Reports Medicine, Nov 5
studies.designAndSize: Systematic review, 247 studies
studies.caveats: Context on clinical translation and independent validation – not a direct test of explainability. Selected journal set (31 titles).
studies.whyItMatters: Many medical AI studies lack independent validation, so care teams should ask for external evidence before adopting a tool.

studies.title: Visible reasoning increased over-reliance
studies.finding: In three online experiments (N = 657) across health, environment, and technology information tasks, showing the model’s reasoning increased over-reliance because it acted as a competence cue. Harder tasks raised over-reliance too.
studies.source: Zhu & Li, Telematics and Informatics, Oct
studies.designAndSize: Three online experiments, N = 657
studies.caveats: Online information tasks, not clinical decisions. The useful line is persuasive generated reasoning versus independently checkable evidence.
studies.whyItMatters: Showing reasoning raised over-reliance by making the AI look competent, so explanations must invite scrutiny, not signal authority.

studies.title: Surgeons accepted wrong AI incisions
studies.finding: In a two-phase experiment, 19 surgeons accepted 60.6% of deliberately wrong AI incision suggestions (43 of 71), and their confidence rose after seeing the AI (Δ +0.65). Oversight has to be designed in.
studies.source: Morais et al., Surgical Endoscopy, Nov 6
studies.designAndSize: Two-phase controlled experiment; 19 surgeons; 231 paired observations; mock AI on static frames
studies.caveats: Mock AI on static video frames, not a live operation.
studies.whyItMatters: Surgeons followed wrong AI suggestions and grew more confident, so oversight and visible reasoning must be built into the tool.

studies.title: Stone-detection AI looks near-perfect in the lab
studies.finding: Across 14 CT studies, pooled sensitivity was 0.967 and specificity was 0.979. Detection studies, the ones closest to real workflows, scored lower (sensitivity 0.935, specificity 0.919).
studies.source: Talyshinskii et al., World Journal of Urology, Nov 5
studies.designAndSize: Diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis of 14 studies
studies.caveats: Most studies lacked external validation and were at high risk of bias.
studies.whyItMatters: Lab results overstate how AI performs in real workflows, so care teams should judge tools on deployment evidence.

studies.title: AI hospital courses matched on quality
studies.finding: Five physicians rated an EHR-connected agent (Gemini 2.5 Pro) against clinician-written hospital courses for 50 Mayo Clinic stays. Overall quality matched (7.27 vs 7.42). The agent's narratives were less complete (0.84 points lower).
studies.source: Lee et al., Circulation: Population Health and Outcomes, Nov 6
studies.designAndSize: Blinded paired rating of 50 cardiology hospitalizations at one site
studies.caveats: A clinician reviews the note before it goes in the record.
studies.whyItMatters: An AI agent matched clinicians on overall quality and left gaps in completeness, so reviewers must see what it omitted.

studies.title: Real citations did not make answers safer
studies.finding: On a 50-question perioperative IBD benchmark, every retrieved PubMed citation was real (236 checks). Retrieval did not reliably make answers more correct or safe: one model's accuracy rose (Δ +0.44) and the other's did not (Δ +0.21, not significant), safety showed no reliable benefit, and faithfulness fell for one model (Δ −0.24).
studies.source: Hu et al., Journal of Multidisciplinary Healthcare, Nov 1
studies.designAndSize: 50-question benchmark; two 8B models; three blinded physician raters
studies.caveats: Showing real sources is not the same as showing sound reasoning.
studies.whyItMatters: Real citations did not guarantee safe answers, so showing sources must come with reasoning clinicians can check.

studies.title: A maternal-health chatbot did not improve outcomes
studies.finding: In a randomized trial of 400 pregnant and postpartum participants followed for 12 months, access to a generative AI chatbot did not improve anxiety, depression, ED visits, or postpartum care versus an active control.
studies.source: Norell et al., JAMA Network Open, Nov 2
studies.designAndSize: Randomized trial; 400 participants; 12-month follow-up
studies.caveats: One trial of a maternal-health chatbot versus an active control.
studies.whyItMatters: A chatbot without a proven clinical pathway did not move maternal outcomes, so AI in care needs outcome evidence.

studies.title: Explained risk scores sharpened foot-ulcer care plans
studies.finding: In a randomized evaluation of 202 patients, physicians using an explainable AI platform that showed the drivers behind each risk score for cure, recurrence, amputation and death wrote higher-quality care recommendations than under usual care: 7.77 vs 6.47 (mean difference 1.30, 95% CI 1.08–1.52). Completeness gained the most.
studies.source: Zhang et al., eClinicalMedicine
studies.designAndSize: Multicentre derivation and validation (763 + 100 patients, three hospitals in China) with a prospective randomized evaluation; 202 patients randomized 1:1, 200 analysed
studies.caveats: Outcome is recommendation quality, not patient health outcomes.
studies.whyItMatters: Showing care teams why a patient is at risk produced more complete care plans – AI that shows its work sharpens clinical judgment.

studies.title: Decide, then consult: juniors closed the gap
studies.finding: Junior anesthesiologists who made an independent decision before consulting DeepSeek-R1 scored 86.0 vs 61.7 on accuracy and 84.3 vs 53.7 on comprehensiveness compared with juniors working alone, with no significant difference from senior experts. They adopted 65% of the AI's suggestions and modified 35%.
studies.source: Yang, Zhang & Wang, BMC Anesthesiology
studies.designAndSize: Simulation-based multi-arm study; 32 junior residents randomized to AI-assisted or unaided; 16 senior experts as a non-randomized comparator; 20 clinical scenarios
studies.caveats: Simulated scenarios; the authors flag automation-bias risk in critical cases.
studies.whyItMatters: Deciding before consulting a reasoning model helped junior clinicians close the gap with seniors, keeping them in the thinking.

studies.title: An interpretable triage model cut time to diagnosis
studies.finding: In a 2-year randomized pragmatic study of 2,385 people with a positive ANA test, inviting the patients an interpretable EHR model flagged as high risk to an expedited rheumatology visit cut median time to autoimmune diagnosis from 138 to 43 days (HR 1.9, 95% CI 1.3–2.7).
studies.source: Barnado et al., NEJM AI
studies.designAndSize: Randomized pragmatic study in one academic health system (Vanderbilt); 2,385 randomized, 1,960 analysed; 2 years
studies.caveats: One health system; it tests faster triage, not how clinicians reason with the model.
studies.whyItMatters: An interpretable model used for triage cut months off diagnosis, showing transparent AI can speed care in practice.

studies.title: LLM answers shifted with the prompt
studies.finding: Across five LLMs and four prompting strategies on 1,455 aortic stenosis patients, GPT-o1 with chain-of-thought reached 97.5% severity accuracy and Grok-2 with chain-of-thought matched 88.3% of real treatment decisions. Performance varied by model, task and prompt, and after adjustment the AI recommendations were not associated with mortality (HR 1.41, 95% CI 0.58–3.45).
studies.source: Huang et al., BMJ Health & Care Informatics
studies.designAndSize: Retrospective evaluation; 5 LLMs × 4 prompting strategies; 1,455 patients with aortic stenosis
studies.caveats: Retrospective, with no clinicians in the loop.
studies.whyItMatters: LLM recommendations shifted with prompt wording, so care tools need standardized, visible reasoning before clinical use.

studies.title: Physicians missed a failing AI
studies.finding: As a heart-sound AI's reliability fell from 90% to 0%, AI-assisted accuracy among 48 physicians fell from 81.45% to 58.33%, below their own unassisted performance. 12.5% noticed the decline unprompted, and having physicians commit to their own answer before seeing the AI did not improve performance.
studies.source: Schlicker et al., npj Digital Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Randomized 2 × 4 mixed-factorial experiment; 48 physicians; 40 heart-sound trials; AI advice before vs after the physician's own call
studies.caveats: Simulated malfunction on recorded heart sounds, not live care.
studies.whyItMatters: Physicians rarely noticed a failing AI and forcing an upfront decision did not fix it – oversight needs tools that surface failure.

studies.title: Physicians would act on false AI abstracts
studies.finding: Twenty emergency and trauma physicians said they would act on 23 of 40 GPT-5 abstracts containing false claims (specificity 43%), and rated true and false abstracts alike for perceived accuracy (3.15 vs 2.88, P = .21).
studies.source: Hakam et al., Journal of Medical Internet Research
studies.designAndSize: Cross-sectional vignette survey; 20 physicians at 4 German hospitals; 80 ratings of 4 GPT-5 abstracts (2 false, 2 accurate)
studies.caveats: Reported intent from 20 physicians, not observed practice.
studies.whyItMatters: Physicians could not tell false AI abstracts from true ones, so AI-generated evidence must show traceable sources.

studies.title: Kansas Zemplee / Windsor Place pilot
studies.finding: 121 Medicaid members who qualified for nursing-home care but lived at home: nursing-facility days fell 54%, depression scores 45% and loneliness scores 29% vs before the pilot. Technology cost under $600 per person per month; 7 of 109 analyzed (about 6%) moved to a nursing home.
studies.source: Zemplee and Windsor Place At-Home Care press release (white paper 'Nursing Homes Without Walls')
studies.designAndSize: Single-arm pilot with before/after comparison; 121 people; partners KU Medical Center, UnitedHealthcare of Kansas; KDADS funding
studies.caveats: Preliminary, vendor-published, not peer-reviewed, no control group. Bundles sensors, vitals monitoring, devices and in-home services, so results can't be pinned on the AI.
studies.whyItMatters: A vendor pilot links remote support at home with fewer nursing-facility days, a signal for caregiver-centered care at home.

studies.title: NYU Caregiver Intervention
studies.finding: Counseling and support for spouse caregivers cut the rate of nursing-home placement by 28.3% (HR 0.717) and delayed it by a model-predicted median of 557 days. Caregiver improvements explained 61.2% of the effect.
studies.source: Mittelman et al., Neurology
studies.designAndSize: Randomized controlled trial; 406 spouse caregivers of people with Alzheimer's; enrolled over 9.5 years
studies.caveats: Volunteer sample of spouse caregivers in one New York program; 557 days is a model-predicted median.
studies.whyItMatters: Supporting the caregiver kept people with dementia at home longer – supporting the caregiver supports the patient.

studies.title: REACH II
studies.finding: A 6-month, 12-session caregiver program improved caregiver quality of life and cut clinical depression (12.6% vs 22.7%). No significant difference in institutionalization at 6 months.
studies.source: Belle et al., Annals of Internal Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Randomized controlled trial; 642 Hispanic, white and Black caregivers in 5 US cities
studies.caveats: Only 6-month follow-up; too short to show placement effects.
studies.whyItMatters: Caregiver support improved caregiver quality of life and depression, with no change in placement at six months.

studies.title: Caregiver mental health and patient survival
studies.finding: Worse caregiver mental health predicted higher patient mortality, even after accounting for diagnosis, age, sex, dementia severity and the patient's own mental health.
studies.source: Lwi et al., PNAS
studies.designAndSize: Prospective cohort; 176 patient-caregiver dyads with neurodegenerative disease
studies.caveats: Small, one center. Association, not proof of cause.
studies.whyItMatters: Caregiver mental health predicted patient survival, tying caregiver support directly to patient outcomes.

studies.title: Caregiver strain and caregiver mortality
studies.finding: Older spousal caregivers who felt strain had a 63% higher risk of dying over 4 years than non-caregivers (RR 1.63). Caregivers without strain had no higher risk.
studies.source: Schulz & Beach, JAMA (Caregiver Health Effects Study)
studies.designAndSize: Prospective population-based cohort; 819 adults aged 66 to 96 living with a spouse (392 caregivers, 427 non-caregivers); about 4.5 years average follow-up
studies.caveats: Observational; confidence interval touches 1.00.
studies.whyItMatters: Strained caregivers face higher mortality, so caregiver support protects the people doing the caring.

studies.title: What predicts nursing-home admission
studies.finding: Across 80 studies, caregivers' emotional stress, wish to institutionalize and feeling 'trapped' predicted nursing-home admission for people with dementia, alongside patient factors.
studies.source: Gaugler et al., Medical Care
studies.designAndSize: Systematic review of 80 studies
studies.caveats: Review of observational studies; predictors, not causes.
studies.whyItMatters: Caregiver stress predicts nursing-home admission, so easing it is a lever for keeping people home.

studies.title: Caregiver burden and ED returns
studies.finding: Each 1-point rise on the Zarit burden scale was linked to 3% higher odds of an ED revisit within 30 days (OR 1.03). No link at 3 or 7 days, or for revisits ending in admission.
studies.source: JAMA Network Open (LEARNING WISDOM cohort, Québec)
studies.designAndSize: Prospective cohort; 1,409 patient-caregiver dyads (patients 65+)
studies.caveats: Small effect with a confidence interval starting at 1.00; COVID-era data.
studies.whyItMatters: Caregiver burden showed a modest link to 30-day ED returns and no link at shorter windows.

studies.title: Caregivers in discharge planning
studies.finding: Bringing family caregivers into discharge planning cut readmissions by 25% at 90 days (RR 0.75) and 24% at 180 days (RR 0.76).
studies.source: Rodakowski et al., Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
studies.designAndSize: Meta-analysis; 15 studies (11 with readmission data)
studies.caveats: Interventions varied a lot between studies.
studies.whyItMatters: Including caregivers in discharge planning cut readmissions by a quarter – supporting the caregiver supports the patient.

studies.title: BRI Care Consultation (Benjamin Rose)
studies.finding: Caregivers had 21% fewer depression symptoms at 12 months (Kaiser trial). In the VA version, caregiver depression symptoms rose 6.8% vs 28.2%, and veterans with more behavioral symptoms had fewer readmissions (1.7 vs 2.5) and fewer return ED visits (2.5 vs 3.5).
studies.source: US Administration for Community Living program summary
studies.designAndSize: One RCT (Kaiser Permanente; size not stated in the summary) and one site-randomized trial (VA Partners in Dementia Care, 328 veterans)
studies.sampleSize: 328 veterans (VA trial); Kaiser trial size not verified
studies.caveats: Use effects showed up only in subgroups; no difference in the chance of any admission or ED visit.
studies.whyItMatters: Care consultation eased caregiver depression and cut some hospital use, with results that varied across settings.

studies.title: Nurse staffing and patient death (US)
studies.finding: Each extra patient per nurse was linked to 7% higher odds of a surgical patient dying within 30 days (OR 1.07) and 23% higher odds of nurse burnout (OR 1.23).
studies.source: Aiken et al., JAMA
studies.designAndSize: Cross-sectional linked data; 10,184 nurses, 232,342 patients, 168 Pennsylvania hospitals
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional; association, not cause.
studies.whyItMatters: Nurse workload tracks with patient deaths and burnout, so easing care-worker burden protects patients.

studies.title: Nurse staffing and death (Europe)
studies.finding: One more patient per nurse raised the odds of in-hospital death within 30 days by 7%; every 10% more bachelor's-trained nurses lowered it by 7%.
studies.source: Aiken et al., Lancet (RN4CAST)
studies.designAndSize: Retrospective observational; 422,730 surgical patients, 300 hospitals, 26,516 nurses surveyed, 9 European countries
studies.caveats: Observational.
studies.whyItMatters: Lighter nurse workloads and more trained nurses meant fewer deaths, linking care-worker support to patient survival.

studies.title: Patients forget most of what's said
studies.finding: 40% to 80% of medical information from clinicians is forgotten immediately, and almost half of what is remembered is wrong.
studies.source: Kessels, Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine
studies.designAndSize: Narrative review
studies.caveats: Figures come from older underlying studies, not new data.
studies.whyItMatters: Patients forget most of what clinicians tell them, so caregivers and clear, reviewable explanations carry the care plan home.

studies.title: Spousal TBI and partner mortality
studies.finding: In 3,281 married pairs followed a median 19.5 years in ARIC, a spouse’s traumatic brain injury was associated with 24% higher mortality in the uninjured partner (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.07–1.43). Dementia and major cardiovascular outcomes were not significant.
studies.source: D’Alonzo et al., JAMA Network Open, Nov 2
studies.designAndSize: Prospective ARIC cohort, 3,281 married pairs
studies.caveats: Observational association – caregiving wasn’t measured. Family health consequence, not proof that cutting caregiver burden lowers mortality.
studies.whyItMatters: A spouse's injury was linked to higher partner mortality, showing how health events ripple through the family.

studies.title: Home hospital did not raise caregiver burden
studies.finding: Among 30 caregivers, home hospital did not raise ZBI-12 burden versus usual hospital care (change 0 vs 1.5 points, P = .269). Caregivers credited strong communication and shared decisions with the care team.
studies.source: Brewster et al., Age and Ageing, Oct 31
studies.designAndSize: Mixed methods within a multicenter rural RCT; ZBI-12 for 30 caregivers; 19 interviews
studies.caveats: 30 caregivers in the burden comparison.
studies.whyItMatters: Caring for a loved one at home did not add burden when the care team communicated well and shared decisions.

studies.title: Digital palliative care at home: active help worked
studies.finding: Across six RCTs (589 patients, 367 caregivers), active digital education improved patients' quality of life and symptoms. Passive quality-of-life monitoring showed no benefit, largely because clinicians seldom used it, and the one trial measuring caregiver quality of life found no effect.
studies.source: Xin et al., BMC Palliative Care
studies.designAndSize: Systematic review and narrative synthesis of 6 RCTs; 589 patients, 367 caregivers
studies.caveats: Six varied trials with no pooled estimate.
studies.whyItMatters: Active digital support improved patients' lives at home while passive monitoring did not – tools must engage people.

studies.title: Daily support messages kept dementia caregivers engaged
studies.finding: In a 12-month NIH trial of 966 African American and Hispanic dementia caregivers receiving daily social-support messages, 82.3% stayed 9 months or more although 86.7% had low digital literacy. Emotional tone improved (Cohen's d = 0.756) and the number of isolated caregivers fell 46.2%.
studies.source: Yoon et al., npj Mental Health Research
studies.designAndSize: NIH Stage II/III two-arm trial, non-randomized (NCT03865498); 966 caregivers; 12 months; AI-scored emotional tone
studies.caveats: Both arms received support, so there is no untreated control.
studies.whyItMatters: Daily digital support kept underserved dementia caregivers engaged for a year and reduced isolation.

studies.title: For-profit hospitals: thinner staffing, more deaths
studies.finding: Across 941 hospitals in 10 states and more than 1.17 million Medicare admissions, for-profit ownership was associated with higher 30-day mortality (0.48 points for surgical and 1.13 points for medical patients). Nurse staffing accounted for 45% and 40% of those gaps, and nurse burnout ran 9 points higher, 67% of it through staffing.
studies.source: McHugh et al., Medical Care
studies.designAndSize: Cross-sectional; 143 for-profit and 798 nonprofit hospitals; >1.17 million Medicare admissions; 17,368 bedside nurses; 2024 data
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional association, not a staffing intervention.
studies.whyItMatters: Understaffing explained a large share of excess deaths at for-profit hospitals – supporting care workers supports patients.

studies.title: Rural caregiver navigation eased burden
studies.finding: In Boise State's free, telephonic Family Caregiver Navigator program for a rural state, caregivers with follow-up scores saw burden fall (Zarit-4 9.56 to 6.88) and depression ease (PHQ-9 7.54 to 4.90). 58% (29 caregivers) reported reduced intent to place their care recipient in a facility.
studies.source: Toevs et al., International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
studies.designAndSize: Pre/post program evaluation; 289 caregivers engaged; 48–50 with paired pre/post scores at 30–90 days
studies.caveats: No control group, and about 50 of 289 caregivers completed follow-up.
studies.whyItMatters: Low-cost navigation eased caregiver burden and reduced intent to move loved ones into facilities.

studies.title: Care Ecosystem at scale improved caregiver well-being
studies.finding: Across 1,186 dementia caregiver–patient pairs at six US health systems, caregivers in the navigator-led Care Ecosystem had lower depression at 12 months (PHQ-9 −0.48, 95% CI −0.71 to −0.25), along with lower anxiety (−0.23), distress (−0.82) and strain (−0.45) and higher self-efficacy (+2.01). Gains were larger for caregivers of people with moderate-to-severe dementia.
studies.source: Guterman et al., Alzheimer's & Dementia
studies.designAndSize: Pragmatic multisite implementation study; 1,186 dyads; six US health systems; 12 months
studies.caveats: Single-arm implementation with no control group.
studies.whyItMatters: Navigator-led dementia care improved caregiver well-being at scale across six health systems – supporting the caregiver supports the patient.

studies.title: Medicare GUIDE model
studies.finding: Medicare pays for dementia care navigation, a 24/7 support line, caregiver training and education, and respite services up to $2,500 a year, in an 8-year model that started July 2024.
studies.source: CMS Innovation Center
studies.designAndSize: Federal payment model (program page)
studies.caveats: Dementia only; available only through participating programs. Shows a payer pays, not what it pays for an app.
studies.whyItMatters: Medicare now pays for dementia caregiver support and respite, a direct answer to who pays.

studies.title: Medicare pays for caregiver training
studies.finding: From 2024, Medicare pays when practitioners train caregivers to help carry out a patient's treatment plan (for example, in dementia).
studies.source: CMS, CY 2024 Physician Fee Schedule final rule fact sheet
studies.designAndSize: Federal payment rule
studies.caveats: Paid to clinicians, not to apps or caregivers.
studies.whyItMatters: Medicare pays clinicians to train caregivers, putting caregiver support inside reimbursed care.

studies.title: Medicaid pays family caregivers
studies.finding: All responding states pay family caregivers through at least one Medicaid home care program, and all cover respite; 44 states allow paying legally responsible relatives through waivers.
studies.source: KFF Medicaid HCBS survey 2025
studies.designAndSize: Survey of state Medicaid programs (all states but Florida responded)
studies.sampleSize: State Medicaid programs; all but Florida responded
studies.caveats: Benefits are optional and may shrink after 2025 federal Medicaid cuts.
studies.whyItMatters: Every responding state pays family caregivers through Medicaid, making public payers a real funding path.

studies.title: What dementia caregivers would pay
studies.finding: 57% of dementia caregivers would pay something for an 8-session in-home program; mean adjusted willingness was $36 per session. Each extra hour of daily help raised it $1.64.
studies.source: Jutkowitz et al., PharmacoEconomics
studies.designAndSize: Willingness-to-pay survey at baseline of an RCT; 226 caregivers
studies.caveats: Stated, not actual, payment; 32% said $0 and 11% refused to answer.
studies.whyItMatters: Most dementia caregivers would pay something for in-home help, showing direct demand for caregiver support.

studies.title: Adult Day Services Plus: will vs able to pay
studies.finding: Median willingness to pay was $90 to $100 per session, but ability to pay was $31.50 to $50. The program cost $433 per dyad a year; payer savings of $1,501 were not statistically significant.
studies.source: Pizzi et al., Innovation in Aging
studies.designAndSize: Cluster-randomized trial; 34 sites; 203 caregivers
studies.caveats: Savings not significant; stated willingness.
studies.whyItMatters: Caregivers valued day services above what they could afford, so payers need to cover the gap.

studies.title: France: value of an hour of care
studies.finding: Caregivers valued an hour of informal care at €12.10; needing care training was tied to higher value, needing respite or support groups was not.
studies.source: Gervès-Pinquié et al., Health Economics Review
studies.designAndSize: Contingent valuation from national surveys; 223 Alzheimer's caregivers
studies.caveats: 2008 data; French setting; cross-sectional.
studies.whyItMatters: Caregivers put a clear price on an hour of care, and training needs raised it.

studies.title: Caregivers already pay a lot
studies.finding: Family caregivers spend an average of $7,242 a year out of pocket, about 26% of their income ($8,978 for dementia caregivers).
studies.source: AARP Caregiving Out-of-Pocket Costs Study
studies.designAndSize: National survey with a diary component
studies.caveats: Survey; most spending is housing and medical.
studies.whyItMatters: Caregivers spend about a quarter of their income on care, so they cannot be the main payer.

studies.title: Employers lose caregivers
studies.finding: 32% of employees had voluntarily left a job because of caregiving responsibilities.
studies.source: Fuller & Raman, The Caring Company (Harvard Business School)
studies.designAndSize: Employee and employer surveys; over 1,500 employees and 301 employer respondents
studies.caveats: Survey; self-reported.
studies.whyItMatters: Employers lose workers to caregiving, giving them a business reason to pay for caregiver support.

studies.title: Unpaid care and lost work
studies.finding: Caregivers give about 45 hours of unpaid care a week (95% CI 31–58). Among employed caregivers, working hours fell 13%, productivity fell 24%, and 30% reported reduced job responsibilities.
studies.source: Allman et al., JCO Global Oncology
studies.designAndSize: Meta-analysis of 59 studies in 16 countries
studies.caveats: Shows the cost of unpaid care, not that anyone will pay for support.
studies.whyItMatters: Unpaid care cuts work hours and productivity, a cost employers and payers share.
